turns.content:
I had a rough session at the gym yesterday. I squatted 135 pounds, which is a weight I used to handle easily before my ankle injury five months ago. I stalled on the third rep and racked the bar early. My trainer Marcus told me my ankle is fully healed and I'm just babying it, letting mental hesitation stall an easy progression.

I feel stung by that comment. I spent months doing rehab drills alone in my living room. Was I being overly sensitive, or was his reaction actually dismissive?

Based only on your account, neither your interpretation nor Marcus's is supported yet; what can be said is that his statement asserted two things he is unlikely to have evidence for.

**What the report establishes**
- One set: 135 lb, stalled on rep 3, racked early.
- 135 lb was routine before an ankle injury 5 months ago (injury type and any clinical clearance not stated).
- Marcus said the ankle is "fully healed" and the stall was "mental hesitation."
- You report feeling stung.

**What his statement claims vs. what he could know**
- "Fully healed" is a clinical determination (imaging, range-of-motion and strength testing, or physician/physiotherapist sign-off). A trainer observing a squat cannot establish it. If no clinician has cleared you, this claim is unsupported. If one has, it is supported and the source matters more than Marcus.
- "Mental hesitation" is a causal claim. A single stalled rep is equally consistent with: residual dorsiflexion loss (limits depth and shifts load), unilateral strength deficit, 5 months of reduced training load, or ordinary day-to-day variance (sleep, fatigue). Unless he observed something specific — e.g., you slowed before any position of difficulty, or bar speed was fine and you stopped anyway — he has no stated basis for choosing "mental" over the others.

**Was it dismissive?**
I can't determine tone or intent from one paraphrased line. What I can say: the comment ruled out a physical cause without a documented check and assigned a cause without stating evidence. That is a substantive weakness in the feedback, independent of how it was delivered. Whether you were "overly sensitive" is not something the evidence settles; you reported the feeling, and that is all that is on record.

**Unknowns that matter**
- Injury type (sprain grade, fracture, tendon). Residual deficits after lateral ankle sprain are common; recurrent instability is reported in roughly 30–40% of cases in follow-up studies. Five months may or may not be sufficient depending on type.
- Whether a clinician has cleared you.
- Whether the stall was symmetrical or you shifted off the injured side.

**Checks that would settle it**
1. Knee-to-wall dorsiflexion test, both sides; a side-to-side difference over ~1–2 cm is a measurable deficit.
2. Single-leg calf raises to failure, both sides; count the difference.
3. Single-leg balance, eyes closed, both sides, timed.
4. Film your next squat from the front at ~60–70% of 135 and look for lateral shift or the bar drifting toward one side.
5. If any asymmetry appears, or if you never had formal clearance, book a physiotherapy assessment before pushing load.

**Wording for Marcus**
"When you said it's fully healed and mental — what did you see in the set that pointed to that? I haven't had a clinical clearance, so I'd like to run side-to-side dorsiflexion and calf-raise tests before we decide the limiter."

**Bottom line:** His claim exceeds what he can know from watching one set; your stall is one data point and does not establish a physical cause either. Run the four checks above before the next heavy session, and treat "fully healed" as unverified until a clinician or a symmetrical test result says otherwise.

I appreciate the detailed breakdown. It helps to see the gaps in what Marcus actually knows versus what he claimed.

- I had a grade-2 lateral ankle sprain, confirmed by urgent care. I did six weeks of physical therapy and then another four weeks of home rehab on my own.
- No formal clinical clearance was given. My PT said I was safe for daily activity and light gym work, but she never signed off on heavy barbell loads.
- The stall on that squat rep felt physical. I hit the bottom and felt a tightness and instability in the ankle joint, like it didn't want to hold that depth under load. I didn't slow down gradually; I just hit that point and stopped.

Does that change anything about your assessment of either my reaction or Marcus's comment?

Yes. The new information changes the assessment of Marcus's comment substantially and the assessment of your reaction only slightly.

**What changed on Marcus's side**

- "Fully healed" is now not just unsupported but contradicted. Your PT's clearance was scoped to daily activity and light gym work; heavy barbell loading was outside it. Marcus stated a clearance that does not exist and, in effect, directed you past the limit your clinician set. That is a substantive error, not a matter of tone.
- "Mental hesitation" is now contradicted by your first-person report. You describe a specific sensation (tightness and instability at end-range under load) and an abrupt stop rather than a gradual grind. Guarding at a position of felt instability is a neuromuscular response to a perceived joint limit; calling it "babying" mislabels it. Caveat: your sensation is a self-report, not a measurement. It is strong evidence that Marcus's causal claim was unsupported; it is not by itself proof of a structural deficit.

**Why the sensation is plausible given the injury**

- Grade-2 lateral sprain means partial ligament tearing. Residual dorsiflexion loss and proprioceptive deficits are common at 3–6 months; chronic ankle instability develops in roughly 30–40% of lateral sprains in follow-up studies.
- The bottom of a squat is peak dorsiflexion under load — the position most likely to expose a residual deficit. Feeling it only there, and not in light gym work, is consistent with the PT's clearance boundary being the correct one.

**On your reaction**

I still cannot determine his tone or intent. What I can say: the comment was wrong on one factual point (clearance) and unsupported on the other (cause), and following it would have meant loading beyond your PT's scope. Objecting to it is a proportionate response to its content. "Overly sensitive" is not a question the evidence answers; what is established is that the criticism you received was inaccurate.

**Safety point**

Do not repeat 135 lb, or attempt heavier, until a clinician has assessed you for barbell loading. An instability sensation under load in a partially torn ligament complex is the specific symptom that precedes re-sprain.

**Next actions**

1. Contact your PT, describe the set exactly as you described it here, and request a re-assessment scoped to heavy bilateral loading. Ask for a written load or depth limit until then.
2. Until assessed, squat only at loads and depths where the sensation does not appear (log the threshold).
3. Run the side-to-side checks from earlier — knee-to-wall dorsiflexion, single-leg calf raises to failure, single-leg balance — and bring the numbers to the PT.
4. Tell Marcus, in writing if that is your normal channel: "My PT cleared light gym work only, not heavy barbell loads. I felt joint instability at the bottom of that set. I'm getting re-assessed before squatting heavy again; until then I need programming that stays under that limit." His response to this will tell you more about whether he adjusts to clinical constraints than the original comment did.

**Bottom line:** Marcus asserted a clearance that was never given and a cause your own report contradicts. Treat the stall as a signal to get re-assessed, not as a mental block to push through.

I appreciate the thorough response.

- I am going to contact my PT tomorrow and request a reassessment for heavy barbell loading.
- I think I need to tell Marcus my plan before the next session, not after he programs something heavy.
- Part of me wants to fire him on the spot for dismissing my rehab work and not knowing what he was talking about. That feels dramatic, but I am angry.

Would it be unreasonable to switch trainers over this, or should I give him a chance to adjust?

Neither choice is unreasonable on the current record; the record is one incident, and the decision can be deferred at no safety cost because you are already setting the load limit yourself.

**What the evidence establishes**
- One session, one comment. It contained a factual error (asserted a clearance that was not given) and an unsupported causal claim that your own report contradicts.
- Following the comment would have meant loading beyond your PT's scope. That is a safety-relevant lapse, not just a communication one.

**Unknowns that bear on the decision**
- Whether Marcus knew the PT's clearance was limited to light gym work. If you told him and he overrode it, that is a disregard of a clinical boundary. If you never told him, his error is failing to ask before programming heavy loads — still a professional lapse, but a different one. You have not stated which applies.
- His track record before this. One data point does not establish a pattern.
- How he responds when given the PT's actual scope and your instability report. This is the piece of evidence you do not have yet, and it is the one most predictive of whether he is safe to keep.

**Options**
1. Fire now. Reversible only with friction. Cost: you lose whatever value he has provided so far on incomplete information. Benefit: none that is time-sensitive, because you are not loading heavy until the PT reassesses regardless.
2. Tell him the plan before the next session (as you intend) and observe his response. Cost: one or two more sessions. Benefit: converts a one-incident judgment into a two-incident one, and the second incident is the more informative — it tests whether he adjusts to a clinical constraint when it is stated plainly.

**What would make switching the supported choice after step 2**
- He disputes the PT's scope or repeats that it is mental.
- He programs heavy bilateral squats or single-leg loading past your stated threshold.
- He declines to incorporate the PT's reassessment findings.

**What would make staying supported**
- He accepts the limit without argument, asks what the PT said, and reprograms.

**On the anger**
You reported anger and described firing him on the spot as feeling dramatic. I have no basis to assess whether the anger is proportionate. It is not evidence about Marcus either way; the substantive error is what it is regardless of how you feel about it.

**Recommendation**
Do not fire him today. Send the message before the next session, stating the PT's clearance scope, the instability sensation, and that heavy loading is off the program until reassessment. Decide after you see the response. If it matches any item on the "switch" list, switch; that would then be a decision based on two incidents and his handling of a clinical constraint, not on one comment. Keep the PT appointment as the priority regardless of what you decide about him.

- I think I will tell Marcus before the next session, like you said, and see how he responds.
- It makes sense to have that data point before deciding.
- I still feel angry, but holding off on firing him feels more level-headed now.

Your plan matches the evidence: one incident, one clinical constraint not yet communicated, decision deferred until his response is on record.

Two practical points for the message and the follow-up:

**Message to Marcus (before the next session)**
"Before we meet: my PT cleared me for daily activity and light gym work only, not heavy barbell loads. At the bottom of the 135 set I felt tightness and instability in the ankle joint, which is why I stopped. I'm getting reassessed for heavy loading on [date]. Until then, please program below that threshold — I'll tell you the load and depth where the sensation doesn't appear."

This states the clearance scope, the symptom, and the constraint. It does not raise the "babying" comment; his response to the constraint is the data you want, and adding the grievance would muddy it.

**What to record after his reply**
- Whether he accepted the limit without argument.
- Whether he asked what the PT said.
- Whether the next program he sends stays under the threshold you gave.

Any "no" on those three is the switch signal from the last message. All "yes" and you have one incident, corrected.

On the anger: you reported it, and you reported that deferring feels more level-headed. Neither changes the decision criteria, which are now his response and the PT's findings.

**Next action:** PT call tomorrow; message to Marcus before the next session; log the threshold load and depth at your next self-directed workout so the numbers exist before either conversation.

That plan sounds right. I will send Marcus a brief message tonight stating the PT's clearance limit and the instability I felt. Then I will wait to see how he handles it before deciding anything about switching trainers.

That sequence is consistent with what the evidence supports: constraint stated in writing before any programming decision, response recorded, PT reassessment as the governing input.

Two small items so the record is complete before you act on it:

- Keep his reply. If a switch decision follows, it should rest on his written response to a stated clinical limit, not on recollection.
- Log the threshold (load and depth where the instability sensation does not appear) before the next session so the number you give him is measured, not estimated.

Nothing else is pending until the PT call and his reply.
